entry.title: Week 7: Where I've actually got to
entry.content:
Week 7 · 16 October 2026 · Data Structures (数据结构), Tsinghua University · XuetangX

Seven weeks in, this site exists and I can say exactly how far into the course I am. Which is not as far as I’d like.

1. What I worked on

Building this site and auditing where I actually am: which sessions happened,
what I covered in each, and what’s still ahead in Chapter 1.

2. What was challenging, and how I handled it

Two things, and neither is about the course content.

The journal wasn’t being written. I’d been doing the sessions but not
recording them, so the entries for weeks 2, 3 and 5 are being written after the
fact. I’ve kept the scope of each session accurate, but the reflections are
reconstructed, and reconstructed reflection is weaker than reflection written on
the day. I’d rather say that here than have it look like I wrote them at the time.
The fix is structural: the entry gets written in the session now, not later.

I haven’t submitted any code. Seven weeks in and I’ve watched lectures and
done exercises, but nothing has gone to the online judge. That’s the part of this
course that actually tests whether I understood something, and I’ve been skipping
it. I think it’s because the videos feel like progress and a rejected submission
feels like failure.

3. How well I ran my own learning

Self-score: 79

Working within structure, not directing it. I’ve turned up and worked each
session, and the course choice in week 1 was mine. But this site only exists
because it was asked for, the journal only got written when it was collected,
and I haven’t once gone past what the video put in front of me. Two of those are
things I could have decided to do myself and didn’t. I’d give myself an 89 on the
sessions where I was actually working through content, and this score is dragged
down by the seven weeks of not journalling.

4. What I’ll do differently next session

Submit something to the judge, even a trivial problem, so the pipeline is tested
before an assignment depends on it. And write the entry before the period ends
rather than after.

Evidence

Sessions so far. VLD is one period a week, on Fridays, and two of those Fridays
were public holidays — Mid-Autumn on 25 September and the National Day make-up on
9 October — so of seven weeks I’ve had five sessions:

DateWeekCovered
4 Sep1Choosing the course
11 Sep2Enrolling, judge setup, 绪论 A 计算
18 Sep3绪论 B1 — measuring algorithms
2 Oct5绪论 B2 — Turing machines
16 Oct7This checkpoint

Where that leaves me in the course. Still inside Chapter 1, 绪论. Done:
计算, and most of 计算模型 — performance measurement, problem size, worst case,
the idealised model, and the Turing machine including the worked example (01B2-2).
Still ahead in this chapter: the RAM model, big-O notation, then iteration and
recursion.

That’s slower than I expected. One period a week turns out to be two or three
lecture videos plus their exercises, and the exercises are where the time goes.

entry.title: Week 5: Turing machines
entry.content:
What I worked on

Where I got stuck

What I’d do differently next time

Next session

Week 5 · 2 October 2026 · Data Structures (数据结构), Tsinghua University · XuetangX

Back after a two-week gap — last Friday was Mid-Autumn Festival, so no class on the 25th.

1. What I worked on

绪论 B2: the Turing machine model and a worked example of one running. Two videos plus tracing through the example on paper.

2. What was challenging, and how I handled it

Coming back after two weeks off was rough. I couldn’t remember where I’d left off and spent the first few minutes scrolling through my notes from week 3. I hadn’t looked at any course material during the break, which is exactly the kind of thing that shows whether you’re self-directing or just following a schedule. I was following the schedule.

The Turing machine itself: tape, read/write head, alphabet, state set, transition function. I can list those now, but during the video I kept forgetting the transition function. A rule like (q, c) → (p, d, L/R) means “if you’re in state q reading character c, write d, move left or right, and switch to state p.” It makes sense when you read it, but when I tried to trace B2-2’s example on paper I kept losing track of which state I was in after each step. I think I was reading the transition table as a sequence of instructions — top to bottom, like code — instead of as a lookup table where you find your current (state, character) pair. Once I started treating it as a lookup table it went much smoother.

The bigger question is why any of this matters. Nobody builds Turing machines. The course spends two full videos on them, and I’ll be honest: during the first video I thought it was a detour. By the end of the second I think I see the point — it’s about defining what “computable” means so you can later say whether a problem is solvable at all, not just slowly. But I’m not fully there yet. I’ll see if it connects to something later.

3. How well I ran my own learning

Self-score: 79

I showed up and did the work, but the two-week break exposed that I’m not doing anything outside of class time. I didn’t review, didn’t look ahead, didn’t try anything on my own during the holiday. That’s “working within structure.” The session itself was fine — I traced the example, caught my own mistake with the transition table, and pushed through the parts I didn’t immediately see the point of. But the overall pattern is still reactive.

4. What I’ll do differently next session

Before class, spend ten minutes reviewing last session’s notes. The two-week gap made it obvious that I forget everything between sessions if I don’t look at it at all. Also: I’m four sessions in and still in Chapter 1. The pace isn’t a problem by itself — the course site says slow is fine — but I want to at least know what’s ahead so I’m not surprised.

Evidence

Paper trace of the B2-2 Turing machine example (not photographed). No OJ submissions — the Turing machine section doesn’t have programming exercises.

entry.title: Week 3: How you measure an algorithm
entry.content:
What I worked on

Where I got stuck

What I’d do differently next time

Next session

Week 3 · 18 September 2026 · Data Structures (数据结构), Tsinghua University · XuetangX

All theory this week — how to measure how good an algorithm is without actually running it.

1. What I worked on

绪论 B1: performance measurement, problem size, worst-case analysis, and the idealised computation model. Four videos and the associated exercises.

2. What was challenging, and how I handled it

The first thing that tripped me up was why you can’t just time your code. I mean, I knew from competitive programming that the same code runs differently on different machines, but I hadn’t thought about it formally. The answer is you count operations instead of seconds, which removes the hardware from the equation. Makes sense, but then you need to define what counts as an “operation,” and that’s where the idealised model comes in.

Writing cost as T(n) instead of a single number was the part that took a bit to get used to. For sorting, n is the number of elements; for multiplying two numbers, n is the number of digits. They’re both called n but they measure completely different things, and the function T means something different in each case. I had to pause the video and think about that for a minute.

Worst-case analysis I actually found intuitive — in competitive programming you always think about the worst input because that’s what gets you TLE. What I hadn’t considered is that this is a deliberate choice, not an obvious truth. You could analyse the average case instead, and sometimes that’s more useful, but worst-case is the default because it gives a guarantee. The course presented it as a modelling decision, which felt more honest than the way I’d been thinking about it.

The idealised model that ignores cache, word length, and memory speed still feels a bit hand-wavy. I get that you need to simplify to say anything general, but I’m not fully convinced that ignoring all hardware details doesn’t sometimes give you the wrong answer in practice.

3. How well I ran my own learning

Self-score: 89

This was my most focused session so far. The content is conceptual and there’s no code to write, which normally makes me zone out, but I stayed with it because I kept finding connections to things I already sort of knew from competitive programming. The gap between “sort of knowing” and actually understanding was bigger than I expected. Not 100 because I only watched and took notes — I didn’t try to come up with my own examples or look ahead at what’s next.

4. What I’ll do differently next session

After each video, close the tab and try to restate the main idea in one sentence before moving on. This week I watched all four in a row and by the end I had to go back to the first one to remember the details.

Evidence

Notes on T(n), worst-case vs average-case, and the idealised model. No OJ submissions yet — this section of the course is all conceptual.

entry.title: Week 2: Setting up, and what “computation” means
entry.content:
What I worked on

Where I got stuck

What I’d do differently next time

Next session

Week 2 · 11 September 2026 · Data Structures (数据结构), Tsinghua University · XuetangX

First real session with the course material. Half of it was setup, the other half was the opening lectures on computation.

1. What I worked on

Enrolled on XuetangX, registered on the Tsinghua online judge with the same email, and got g++ working locally with -std=c++14. Then watched 绪论 A — the videos on what “computation” actually means.

2. What was challenging, and how I handled it

Setting up the OJ took longer than it should have. I didn’t realise the account email had to match the XuetangX one, so I registered with the wrong email first and had to redo it. Not hard, just annoying — and it’s the kind of thing I should have read the instructions for before clicking.

The lecture content was unexpected. I came in expecting code and got rope computers and straightedge constructions. My first reaction was “why am I watching this,” but by the end of the video I got the point: these are examples of “basic operations” in different computational models, and the whole idea of analysing algorithms depends on agreeing what counts as one step. It clicked when he showed that a straightedge can do addition, because I’d never thought of geometry that way.

The four properties of an algorithm — correctness, determinism, feasibility, finiteness — I can list them now, but during the video I kept mixing up feasibility and finiteness. Feasibility means each step is actually doable; finiteness means it stops. The Hailstone sequence was the example that made this stick: it’s a perfectly valid program, it runs, every step is simple, but nobody can prove it always terminates, so it’s not an algorithm. I thought the distinction was a bit academic at first, but it’s actually kind of interesting that such a simple program is an open problem.

3. How well I ran my own learning

Self-score: 89

I got through everything I planned and made a real attempt to understand the concepts rather than just watching. But I spent the first twenty minutes on setup that I could have done at home the night before. If I’d done that, I would have had time to try the first OJ problem. Managing my learning, not directing it yet.

4. What I’ll do differently next session

Do any setup or admin stuff outside class time. The period is only 45 minutes — that’s two or three videos plus exercises if I don’t waste any of it.

Evidence

Registered on XuetangX and the OJ (no screenshots taken at the time). Notes from 绪论 A on the four algorithm properties and the Hailstone example.

entry.title: Week 1: Picking the course took longer than I thought it would
entry.content:
Week 1 · 4 September 2026 · Data Structures (数据结构), Tsinghua University · XuetangX

This session was deciding what my VLD actually is. The direction was never in question — data structures and algorithms, in C++ — but which course turned out to be a real decision.

1. What I worked on

Comparing four candidate courses and committing to one: Tsinghua University’s
Data Structures (数据结构), taught by Prof. Deng Junhui, free on XuetangX. I also
read through what the course assumes you already know, and found the online judge
where the programming assignments get submitted.

2. What was challenging, and how I handled it

The hard part was that every obvious option had a catch, and I couldn’t tell
which catch mattered until I worked out what I actually needed.

  • Stanford CS106B — everything’s public and it’s in C++, but nothing I submit
    gets marked. I’d be writing code into a void.
  • UC San Diego’s specialisation on Coursera — properly graded, but it needs a
    financial-aid application, and it mixes Python, Java and C++.
  • UIUC Accelerated CS Fundamentals — C++, free to audit, closest to a drop-in
    answer. But about 60 hours total, which is thin for a whole year.
  • Tsinghua’s 数据结构 — free, entirely C++, and it has a real online judge.

So I wrote down the three things I actually needed — work that gets graded, C++
throughout, and no cost — and only one option had all three. That’s how I got
unstuck: the comparison was impossible until I’d decided what I was comparing on.

The other difficulty was one I nearly didn’t notice. My first instinct was to
skip a course entirely and just grind problems on USACO Guide and CSES. It’s
tempting because you get a green tick every twenty minutes and it feels like
progress. I talked myself out of it: problem sets teach you to recognise patterns
you’ve already seen, and I’d have spent a year getting faster at things I already
half-know. Being honest, I think I was also avoiding the Tsinghua course because
it’s intimidating — the prerequisites list templates, virtual methods, induction
and expected value, and I’m shaky on at least half of that.

3. How well I ran my own learning

Self-score: 89

I made a real decision and I can defend it, which is more than I’d have managed
if I’d just picked the first free course. But I spent a good chunk of the period
reading course pages without writing anything down, and the comparison only got
fast once I’d listed my criteria. That should have been the first five minutes,
not the last ten. Not 100, because I needed to catch myself drifting rather than
noticing it straight away.

4. What I’ll do differently next session

Send Mr. Wright the course link and my one-sentence reason before I do anything
else, then enrol and register on the judge in the same session — registration
needs to use the same email as the XuetangX account or the grades don’t sync, and
I’d rather get that right once than fix it later.

Evidence

The course comparison above, and the full set of links on my
Resources page.
